projects.title: Nativify
projects.description: Java to native protection powered by LLVM, built to make reverse engineering harder.
projects.content:
This is probably one of the largest projects I've ever worked on, although it started with a much smaller ambition. Back in middle school, a few friends and I wanted to protect the Java software we were building. We tried adding layers of obfuscation, but the underlying program was still there for somebody patient enough to reconstruct. Once we understood how those protections could be reversed, piling on another layer started to feel like postponing the same problem.

That pushed us toward native compilation. If we could translate the Java bytecode into machine code and link it back into the JVM at runtime, somebody trying to understand our software would have a much harder job. Finding a usable implementation was another matter. A lot of the open source projects we looked at were essentially wrapping a JAR inside a DLL, with the bytecode still tucked away inside. Commercial tools like JNIC went further, but the licenses we were looking at cost over $200 a year. That was enough money to make a few middle school students decide they should probably write a compiler.

We started digging into the relationship between the JVM and native code, eventually figuring out how to translate Java bytecode into LLVM intermediate representation. That gave LLVM something it could optimize and compile into real machine code. Getting the whole thing to execute felt enormous, right up until we measured it: our first implementation ran roughly 200 times slower than the original Java application. We had solved enough of the translation problem to discover how much of the performance problem we didn't understand.

That discovery became the next five years of the project. I kept researching compilers and studying how our translated code behaved at runtime, eventually writing a research paper on optimizing the approach. Gradually, we brought the overhead down until our application ran with almost no performance difference. By then, Nativify had grown far beyond the protection tool we'd originally wanted. I was obsessed with the machinery underneath it, and every improvement made me want to understand the next bottleneck. Somehow, trying to save $200 had turned into a very expensive hobby in terms of sleep.

and the epic journey continues...

projects.title: Artorize
projects.description: Protecting digital art with invisible watermarks, perceptual fingerprints, and image processing.
projects.content:
When artists began protesting the use of their work in AI training, I wondered what they could actually do about it. They had spent years developing their craft, only to find their work being collected and used to train models without their permission. Staying off the internet was hardly a solution. Artists needed a place to share their work, and I did not think they should have to give that up to protect it.

I began reading research on adversarial perturbations, small changes to images that could interfere with how AI models learned from them. I had little faith that we could stop companies from scraping the internet, so I thought the better approach was to make the collected data less useful. The research was promising, but most of the tools remained confined to laboratories and GitHub repositories. An artist had to download models, install dependencies, and run everything locally. That seemed an unreasonable burden.

So I built Artorize, bringing these methods into a web application where artists could protect their images without understanding the machinery behind them. Much of the work went into making the models and image-processing pipeline accessible through a simple interface, while keeping the artwork visually intact. I wanted the artist to spend time on the drawing, not on getting a piece of research software to run.

and the epic journey continues...

projects.title: NanoTech Pharma
projects.description: A digital presence for precision nanomedicine, making complex drug delivery science approachable.
projects.content:
Some friends and I began building a website for NanoTech Pharma, a pharmaceutical company working with advanced drug-delivery technologies. We started with Webflow because it was convenient, but soon found ourselves spending more time working around the editor than building what we wanted. The company worked with structures that existed in three dimensions, and I thought the website ought to show something of that. A flat illustration could explain the science, but it could not always give someone a sense of the objects themselves.

Around that time, I began experimenting with AI agents for frontend development. I had used AI to help write code before, but I was surprised by how easily it could help construct and integrate interactive 3D models. It became possible to try ideas that would otherwise have taken considerable time to build. Still, making something move on a screen was not the same as making a good website. Some effects looked impressive on their own but felt out of place beside the text. Others distracted from the science they were supposed to explain.

I kept adjusting the movement, scale, and placement of the elements, trying to give the website some depth without making it feel artificial. The agents could produce a great deal of code, but they had little sense of when enough was enough. That part still required someone to look at the page and decide what ought to stay.

and the epic journey continues...

projects.title: Aeternus Argus
projects.description: Machine learning for encrypted network traffic classification, using XGBoost and Optuna.
projects.content:
I began Aeternus Argus with Mary Conte, a Georgia Tech scholar, to investigate a question in network security. As more internet traffic became encrypted, inspecting the contents of packets was becoming less useful. But encryption did not conceal everything. Packets still arrived at certain intervals, carried different amounts of data, and left patterns of activity and silence. We wondered whether those patterns were enough for a machine to distinguish VPN traffic from ordinary traffic.

We began collecting datasets and examining the information that remained visible. I used XGBoost to build a classifier, though I soon found that training the model was only a small part of the work. The datasets came from different scenarios, their labels were not always consistent, and some features needed considerable cleaning before they could be used. I had to understand what the numbers meant before asking a machine to learn from them.

Once the data was prepared, I began experimenting with cross-validation, feature selection, and hyperparameter tuning through Optuna. Some configurations gave better results than others, but a higher accuracy did not always tell me why. I spent more time studying feature importance, classification thresholds, and the differences between training and evaluation results. It was my first serious encounter with machine learning, and I found that getting a model to produce an answer was considerably easier than understanding whether that answer deserved to be trusted.

and the epic journey continues...

projects.title: Gibbsiq
projects.description: QUBO and Ising optimization with Gibbs sampling, exact verification, and diagnostics you can inspect.
projects.content:
I came across Extropic in a YouTube video and was struck by what they were trying to do. We kept building larger computing facilities, supplying them with more electricity, and spending enormous amounts of energy trying to keep them cool. I could not see how this approach would scale forever. Extropic was working on something different, using the natural fluctuations of physical systems to perform probabilistic computation. I thought there was something remarkable about making use of the very behavior that conventional computers spent so much effort trying to suppress.

I began experimenting with their THRML framework, studying block-Gibbs sampling and how combinatorial problems could be expressed as QUBO and Ising models. But I soon ran into a difficulty. A stochastic solver might return a good solution once, and I had no way of knowing whether it would do so again. The result depended on the model, its constraints, the sampling process, and a good deal of randomness. Looking at the final answer alone told me very little about what had happened.

So I began building Gibbsiq, an optimizer with diagnostics at its center. I added exact enumeration for small problems, checks for constraint penalties, and statistical measures such as effective sample size and split R-hat to examine whether the sampling chains had explored the solution space properly. I also built a qualification system that preserved experimental settings and compared repeated executions against known references. I wanted to be able to find the reason behind an unreliable result, rather than simply run the solver again and hope for a better one. After all, I would never trust ordinary code without tests, and I saw no reason to make an exception for code that happened to use randomness.

and the epic journey continues...

projects.title: PhotonicEngine
projects.description: Advanced ray tracing for Minecraft, bringing together ReSTIR lighting, denoising, and rendering performance.
projects.content:
I began PhotonicEngine because I wanted to understand how modern graphics engines produced realistic light. I had seen what ray tracing could do in games, and I was fascinated by how a computer could calculate reflections, shadows, and indirect illumination quickly enough to produce dozens of frames every second. I knew it would be difficult, but I had not expected the work to take me through so many different fields.

I began by studying existing ray-tracing implementations and adapting newer techniques into the renderer. There was the mathematics of rays and surfaces, the physics of light, and the probability behind sampling it. Then there was the GPU, which had its own way of doing things, and the game engine that had to move data between the CPU and GPU without slowing everything down. Much of the work was written in GLSL, which I found harder than I expected. A shader could compile without an error and still produce an image that was entirely wrong. Sometimes the lighting looked correct in one frame but left traces of itself in the next.

I tried using AI assistants, but they were far less useful here than in ordinary programming. There was little familiar code for them to draw from, and many of their suggestions looked reasonable until I actually ran them. I had to work through the mathematics myself and learn how each part of the rendering pipeline affected the next.

Eventually I began building tests for the things I could measure. I wrote benchmarks for individual GPU passes and automated scenes where I could place and remove a block while recording how the lighting responded. I studied how quickly the denoiser adapted, whether the image converged, and how much computation was being spent on each frame. A screenshot might look beautiful while hiding a dozen problems underneath it. I wanted to understand those problems, one at a time, and find out how much further the renderer could be pushed.

and the epic journey continues...
